verses.text: Hecate stands beside whoever she chooses and gives them powerful help.
In the public assembly, she makes whoever she favors stand out.
And whenever men arm themselves for war that destroys lives,
the goddess stands beside those she chooses,
eager to grant them victory and glory.
She sits beside respected kings as they give judgment.
She is a good helper, too, when men compete in games:
there the goddess stands beside them and lends her aid.
The winner, victorious through might and strength, wins a fine prize
and carries it off with ease and joy, bringing glory to his parents.
She is good at helping riders, too, whenever she chooses.
And for those who work the gray, rough sea
and pray to Hecate and the thundering Earth-shaker, Poseidon,
the glorious goddess easily grants a great catch,
and easily takes it away when it comes in sight, if her heart desires.
With Hermes, she is good at making livestock thrive in their pens.
Herds of cattle and great herds of goats,
and flocks of woolly sheep, if her heart desires,
she makes grow from few to many, or dwindle from many to few.
So, though Hecate is her mother's only child,
she holds honored privileges among all the immortal gods.
Zeus, the son of Cronus, made her nurse of the young who, after her,
opened their eyes to the light of far-seeing Dawn.
So from the beginning she has nursed the young. These are her honors.
Rhea lay with Cronus and bore glorious children:
Hestia, Demeter, and Hera with her golden sandals;
mighty Hades, who lives in halls beneath the earth
with a pitiless heart; and the thundering Earth-shaker, Poseidon;
and Zeus, wise in planning, father of gods and humans,
whose thunder makes the wide earth shake.
Great Cronus swallowed them, each one
as it came from its mother's sacred womb to her knees.
His purpose was to keep any other glorious descendant of Uranus
from holding royal honor among the immortal gods.
For he had learned from Gaia and starry Uranus
that he was destined to be overcome by his own son,
strong though he was, through the plans of great Zeus.
So Cronus kept a sharp watch, and as he waited,
he swallowed his own children. Rhea was gripped by grief that would not fade.
But when Rhea was about to bear Zeus, father of gods and humans,
she begged her own dear parents,
Gaia and starry Uranus,
to help her devise a plan so she could give birth in secret
to her dear child and win vengeance for her father
and for the children great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, had swallowed.
Gaia and Uranus listened closely to their dear daughter and agreed to help.
They told her all that fate had in store
for King Cronus and his strong-hearted son.
They sent her to Lyctus, in the fertile land of Crete,
when she was about to bear her youngest child,
great Zeus. Vast Gaia received him from her
to nourish and care for him on the broad island of Crete.
Gaia came there carrying him through the swift, black night,
first to Lyctus. Taking him in her arms, she hid him
in a deep cave, in the hidden places of the holy earth,
on Mount Aegeum, thickly covered with forest.

uncertainties: 481–482: The Greek does not name the female figure carrying and hiding Zeus. I take her to be Gaia, the preceding subject, though Rhea is also a possible reading.
